query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles, rapid thermal shock synthesis that maximizes lattice distortion (and thus promotes sluggish atomic diffusion) is the dominant factor preserving uniform composition and structural integrity during prolonged high‐temperature operation, independent of additional support anchoring effects. Nanoparticles synthesized with rapid, brief heating will show reduced elemental segregation during catalytic/thermoelectric aging compared to those subjected to longer high-temperature annealing, even when both are deposited on inert supports that minimize substrate anchoring.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly annealed multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles synthesized via thermal shock (e.g., by a rapid MC+MD‐inspired protocol) with pronounced lattice distortion and high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of identically composed nanoparticles differing only in their thermal treatment—one set using a rapid, brief high-temperature shock and one set using extended high-temperature annealing—to modulate the degree of lattice distortion and atomic mobility. Deposit both sets on an inert oxide support (e.g., Al2O3) that minimizes chemical anchoring effects.
generation.conditions: Prolonged exposure/annealing at catalytic or thermoelectric service temperatures between 773 K and 1173 K under inert or mildly reactive atmospheres (to avoid oxidation complications).
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of lattice distortion induced by rapid thermal shock, which creates high diffusion barriers (i.e., sluggish diffusion), serves as the mediator that kinetically 'freezes' the uniform elemental mixing.
generation.mechanism: Rapid thermal shock creates a high-entropy, highly distorted lattice structure where atomic mobility is suppressed, preventing elemental segregation even under prolonged high temperatures. In contrast, extended annealing allows atoms to overcome diffusion barriers, leading to phase separation. By using an inert support, the influence of substrate anchoring is minimized so that differences can be attributed primarily to intrinsic kinetic stabilization via lattice distortion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under prolonged high-temperature conditions, nanoparticles synthesized by rapid thermal shock will retain a more uniform elemental distribution, maintain smaller and more consistent sizes, and show fewer secondary phases compared to those processed via extended annealing—even when both are on inert supports. This outcome evidences that intrinsic kinetic constraints (sluggish diffusion from lattice distortion) are the primary stabilizing factor.
generation.baseline: The baseline is established by nanoparticles typically synthesized via rapid thermal shock on defect-rich carbon supports, where both lattice-induced sluggish diffusion and substrate anchoring contribute to stability. The new experiment on inert oxide supports isolates the contribution of lattice distortion by removing strong anchoring effects.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for near‐equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles operating up to approximately 1173 K in environments with minimal oxidation; effects might differ for nanoparticles with non-equiatomic compositions or in highly reactive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines findings from PMC7069714 (which demonstrated that entropy-induced sluggish diffusion stabilizes the nanoparticle structure at 773 K via MC+MD simulations) and PMC7733500 (which highlighted substrate anchoring on carbon supports for thermal stability). The new element is isolating the intrinsic kinetic stabilization (lattice distortion/sluggish diffusion) by using an inert support to decouple the anchoring effect. The quantitative contribution of each mechanism remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles (with near-equiatomic composition) deposited on an inert oxide substrate (e.g., high-purity Al2O3). One group is synthesized by rapid thermal shock (to maximize lattice distortion) and the other by extended high-temperature annealing (to allow increased atomic mobility). Subject both groups to prolonged annealing at 1173 K for a duration relevant to catalytic operation. Characterize the samples before and after annealing using high-resolution TEM (including elemental mapping), X-ray diffraction, and possibly in situ diffusion measurements.
measurements: Particle size distribution and morphology via TEM
Elemental distribution and segregation analysis via STEM-EDS mapping
Phase identification via XRD to detect emergence of secondary phases or ordering
Measurement of diffusion coefficients (if possible) using tracer techniques or simulation correlations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both groups (rapid shock and extended annealing) show statistically similar degrees of elemental homogeneity, particle size stability, and phase retention after prolonged high-temperature exposure on the inert support, then the hypothesis that rapid shock-induced lattice distortion (and thus sluggish diffusion) is the dominant factor in preserving stability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To investigate the thermal stability of the HEA NPs produced, the samples were annealed at 1173 K (900 °C) for 72 h using a tube furnace with a continuous flow of argon. Their XRD patterns are shown in Supplementary Fig. 12 (Supplementary Note 1). After the annealing, the main phase (single FCC structure) of the HEA NPs still remained unchanged without peak splitting or new peak appearances, suggesting that dealloying or segregation of the constituent elements is minimal in both samples. However, a few minor phases with crystalline structures newly appeared. Based on the peak identification, it seems that those are most probably various oxide phases such as Cr2O3. Other minor phase is also observable with HEA-H2 sample which might be from formation of Co7Mo6 or Fe7Mo6 intermetallic phase while this phase is absent in HEA-He sample suggesting different stabilities of the HEA NPs. This is attributable to the higher crystallinity of HEA-He sample. Overall, the HEA NPs produced by the plasma process are thermally stable even in a high-temperature environment of above 1000 K for an extended period of time.

We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D). cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT). High temperatures are expected to be detrimental to the nanoclusters’ stability, since the nanoparticles would fuse into larger particles to reduce the surface energy at elevated temperatures.
